extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, field entomologists, and readers of natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for collecting, observing, and reporting insects and related natural-history observations during field expeditions. Emphasizes careful live observation, quantitative collecting records, descriptive behavioral sequences, and environmental context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminous insect observation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Record qualitative and quantitative features of bioluminescence: colour, pattern of flashes, timing between rings, response to irritation, persistence after death. (Original phrasing: "the light has been of a well-marked green colour." "The flash was almost co-instantaneous in the two rings..." "When the insect was decapitated the rings remained uninterruptedly bright...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note colour and intensity, whether flashes are voluntary or involuntary, how irritation affects brilliance, temporal sequence (which ring lights first), whether luminous material is fluid/adhesive, and how long luminescence persists post-mortem. Report differences between larvae and adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain live specimens for behavioural study
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep specimens alive for extended observation to reveal feeding and attachment behaviours. (Original phrasing: "I kept several of them alive for some time: their tails are very singular organs... I repeatedly fed them on raw meat; and I invariably observed...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain live specimens when possible, provide naturalistic food, observe repeated behaviours (e.g., tail applied to mouth), record limitations of behaviour in captivity, and report any regular sequences or failures (e.g., tail cannot find mouth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentally test insect mechanics by manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple experimental manipulations to expose mechanical function (e.g., place elater on its back to observe springing mechanism). (Original phrasing: "The elater, when placed on its back and preparing to spring, moved its head and thorax backwards... the spine, by the full action of the muscles, was bent like a spring...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform controlled manipulations (positioning, irritation, restraint) to reveal structures (spines, sheaths) and their roles. Distinguish muscular action from elastic/mechanical components and describe sequence of movements and points of contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record climate and microclimate variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure and report environmental data (temperature, rainfall, dew point, wind, atmospheric haze). (Original phrasing: "The mean temperature, from observations taken at nine o'clock, both morning and evening, was only 72 degs." "In the interval, the difference between the dew point and temperature had increased from 7.5 to 17 degs." "One morning, in the course of six hours, 1.6 inches of rain fell.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include times of observation, arithmetic means when relevant, rainfall amounts and durations, dew-point/temperature differences, prevailing winds, and qualitative descriptions (e.g., 'thin vapour' or haze). Relate climate notes to biological observations where pertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify abundance by individuals rather than only species
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing faunas, emphasise counts of individual organisms as well as species richness. (Original phrasing: "I do not here refer to the number of different species, but to that of the individual insects; for on this it is that the most striking character in the entomology of different countries depends.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both species lists and counts of individuals to characterise ecological dominance and relative importance of orders/families. Use individual abundance to support comparative statements about faunal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document collection counts and taxonomic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete collecting data and taxonomic breakdowns (e.g., numbers of species per order). (Original phrasing from footnote: "one day's (June 23rd) collecting... I caught sixty-eight species of that order. Among these, there were only two of the Carabidae, four Brachelytra, fifteen Rhyncophora, and fourteen of the Chrysomelidae.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give date-stamped collecting tallies, include counts per order/family, and note sampling effort/context (e.g., not attending particularly to Coleoptera). These concrete numbers support broader ecological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe detailed behavioural sequences in situ
rubrics_metrics.description: Record step-by-step sequences of predator–prey and other interactions as observed in nature. (Original phrasing: description of a wasp hunting a spider: "The wasp made a sudden dash at its prey, and then flew away... returned... inflicted two stings... proceeded to drag away the body.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronicle the full sequence (approach, attacks, evasive moves, searching behaviour, inspection with antennae, handling of prey), include timings and spatial context, and note any hesitations or unexpected behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document plant–insect associations and effects of introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Record host-plant relationships and note how human introductions can disrupt these associations. (Original phrasing: "We here see in two distant countries a similar relation between plants and insects of the same families... When man is the agent in introducing into a country a new species, this relation is often broken.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific plant–insect pairings (e.g., beetles attracted to Phallus fungus), report feeding or attraction, and discuss biogeographic/anthropogenic changes that alter these interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and report unusual morphological or behavioural traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight and describe anomalous or unique traits that depart from common expectations (e.g., a butterfly that 'uses its legs for running' or produces a clicking noise). (Original phrasing: "This is the only butterfly which I have ever seen, that uses its legs for running... a clicking noise...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise novel observations, attempt to relate them to structure or mechanism (cite other observers when relevant), and recommend further morphological examination to explain the trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document web architecture, spacing, and gregarious habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Record details of web construction, placement, and communal arrangements among spiders. (Original phrasing: "The webs were placed vertically... separated from each other by a space of about two feet, but were all attached to certain common lines... the tops of some large bushes were encompassed by the united nets.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe web geometry (circular, wedge-shaped segment), attachment points, any reinforcement (zigzag ribbons), spacing between webs, communal lines linking webs, and note if individuals are of similar size/age to infer gregariousness.
